title: Watchfulness
hookLine: guarding thoughts at the door of the heart

cards: A householder is leaving on a long journey. He hands each servant their work, and to one, the porter, he gives a single job: watch the door. That's a short parable in Mark's Gospel.
You don't know when the master will be back, Jesus says. Evening, midnight, cockcrow, morning. So stay awake.

He's speaking privately to four disciples on the Mount of Olives, and then he widens it past them: "And what I say unto you I say unto all, Watch." Yesterday, the heart. Today, the porter who stands at its door.
The Orthodox teachers of prayer have a Greek word for his job: nepsis. Watchfulness.

teach.b: Nepsis is the opposite of drunk. It's being sober, clear, awake.

Peter's first letter has the same pair of ideas, in the King James: "Be sober, be vigilant; because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour." Sober and vigilant together.
The teachers gathered in a collection called the Philokalia make much of it, and one of their pictures is a door. Thoughts come knocking all day long. Plenty are harmless: lunch, the weather, a song.
Some aren't: a resentment, a craving, a cutting reply. Watchfulness doesn't mean you'll never have the thought. It means you see it at the door, before you've let it in and given it a chair.
Some of these writers trace how a bad thought takes over. First it knocks. Then you start talking with it.
Then you agree with it. Then it's running the house. The earlier you notice, the easier the door is to close.

teach.h: KEEP THY HEART WITH ALL DILIGENCE.
teach.b: Proverbs has the same instinct: "Keep thy heart with all diligence; for out of it are the issues of life." Keep, as in guard. Everything that comes out of a life passes through that door first.
So yesterday and today belong together. The prayer of the heart brings you home. Watchfulness keeps the house.
You can't guard a door you never stand near. And a person at rest in the heart is in a good spot to see who's knocking.

how: In Orthodox spiritual life, watchfulness is practiced alongside the Jesus Prayer: monks and lay people learn, often with a spiritual father or mother, to notice thoughts early and turn back to prayer.

o: a deep sleep the desert monks prayed in
fasting from food and drink for a day
a sober, wakeful watch over your thoughts

games.q: watching the door — tap the pairs.
p: keep thy heart with all diligence

s: watchfulness means never having a bad thought
thoughts will knock. watchfulness sees them at the door before they're let in.
in Mark, the call to watch reaches past the four disciples with Jesus
he widens it: what I say unto you I say unto all, Watch.
the earlier you notice a thought, the harder it is to turn away
some of these teachers say the opposite: the earlier you notice, the easier the door is to close.

games.q: a resentful thought about a coworker knocks while you're praying. what does watchfulness ask?
o: argue it out in your head until you win.
see it at the door, name it, and turn back to prayer.
games.why: the watchful writers trace a thought from a knock, to a conversation, to agreement. seeing it early keeps it at the door.

practice: Let your attention settle in your chest again, and watch the door.
When a thought comes, don't chase or fight it; name it quietly, planning, worrying, wanting, remembering, and go back to watching, and if you pray, bring the hard ones before God.
If a thought of harming yourself knocks, please don't sit alone with it: call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.

wordCard.voice: Nepsis. Watchfulness: a sober, wakeful attention that stands at the door of the heart and sees each thought as it comes.

orig.note: Greek, a word for sobriety and watchfulness, used by the writers of the Philokalia.

carryVoice: Your line: guard the door. Knocking isn't the same as coming in. See you tomorrow.
